newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FOCUS-Taiwan dollar ends at 8-yr low; seen falling.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Taiwan dollar ends at 8-yr low; seen falling.

text.p: The Taiwan dollar on Tuesday sank to its lowest close in more than eight years against the U.S. currency after the central bank abandoned its long defence of T$28 to the U.S. dollar.
Shortly after the market closed, the bank said Taiwan's currency was merely reflecting the greenback's strength overseas and vowed it would continue to let market forces determine the exchange rate.
Analysts said the central bank, eager to boost the island's export-driven economy, was likely to allow the local currency to ease as long as the depreciation did not turn into a freefall.

The recently depreciating local unit tested below T$28 shortly after the opening and -- as the bank's non-interference became apparent -- promptly sank to an intra-day low of T$28.20 before recovering mildly to end the day at T$28.170.

The rate marked the exchange rate's lowest level since it traded in the T$28-29 range in 1988, and represented a 2.4 percent dropoff from the central bank's previous long-time defence level at T$27.5.

The bank had defended T$27.5 for some seven years -- even in 1995-96 when communist China menaced rival Taiwan with months of military drills and unarmed ballistic missile tests, sparking a flight to greenbacks, gold and other safe havens.
But analysts said while the central bank felt the need to defend its currency during the military crisis, it would not fret over the Taiwan dollar's current market-driven fall.

"The fall on Tuesday mainly reflected the U.S. dollar's strength overseas rather than factors the central bank considers unhealthy, like rampant speculation or political tension," said Daniel Chen, chief economist for Chinatrust Commercial bank.
In an interview with Reuters Financial Television, Citibank Taiwan chief treasurer Morris Li said: "The Taiwan dollar definitely will shoot into the T$28.5 or even the T$29 level."
Analysts said Taiwan's economic conditions justified a cheaper currency.
The island's inflation was 1.84 percent in June and was forecast by the government to grow a low 2.01 percent for the whole of 1997.

The economy broke out of a 1995-96 slump by posting strong 6.83 percent gross domestic product growth in the first quarter that was triggered in part, analysts said, by the central bank's abandoning of the T$27.5 defence in an export-boosting move.
It was exports, which registered only a mild 2.7 percent growth in June to US$9.959 billion, that the central bank wanted to boost by letting the Taiwan dollar fall, analysts said.
"The economy really cannot be hurt significantly by a fall in the Taiwan dollar, but it can benefit from a fall, especially exports," Chen said.
The central bank vowed to adopt a hands-off policy.
"The central bank will respect market forces and allow the market to determine the exchange rate," the bank said in a statement.

Both the central bank and private analysts said the Taiwan dollar was not vulnerable to the kind of speculative attacks that have beset other Asian currencies like the Thai Baht and the Philippine peso.

"Most of these countries adopt a U.S. dollar-based floating rate, do not have large foreign exchange reserves and have large amounts of debts," the central bank said. "The situation in our country is different."
Citibank's Li agreed. "In terms of the quality of economic fundamentals, we are much, much stronger than other Asian currencies."
Taiwan's central bank boasts imposing foreign exchange reserves of US$90.008 billion -- third largest in the world after Japan and China.
